questions.q: With strict on, why is the variable in catch (error) typed unknown?
questions.explain: Anything can be thrown: strings, objects, null, numbers. TypeScript has no throws clause, and almost any line (including code in libraries) can throw. So the only honest type is unknown, which forces you to check before you use it.
options: Because TypeScript cannot type-check code inside a catch block
Because JavaScript can throw any value, and TypeScript has no way to know what a call might throw
Because Error objects lose their type when they are thrown
Because unknown is faster to check than Error

questions.q: An old project compiles catch (error) { console.log(error.message) } without complaint. Which setting explains that?
questions.explain: useUnknownInCatchVariables, part of strict since TypeScript 4.4, makes catch variables unknown. Without it they are any, and every property access compiles, including ones that crash at runtime.
options: useUnknownInCatchVariables is off (or strict is off), so the catch variable is any
noImplicitAny is on, so the catch variable is Error
skipLibCheck is on, so errors are not checked
The target is too old to support unknown

questions.q: Which catch clause does TypeScript accept?
questions.explain: A catch variable may only be annotated unknown or any (error TS1196 otherwise). A more specific annotation would be a promise nothing checks, because the try block can throw anything.

questions.q: What is wrong with catch (error) { log((error as Error).message) }?
questions.explain: An assertion changes the type, never the value. If null was thrown, .message throws a TypeError inside your error handler; if a string was thrown, it logs undefined. Narrow with instanceof Error or normalize instead.
options: Nothing: as Error converts the value into an Error
It does not compile, because unknown cannot be asserted
It compiles even when null or a string was thrown, and then crashes or logs undefined
It makes the stack trace disappear

questions.q: A catch handles RangeError and then ends with throw error;. Why is that last line important?
questions.explain: Handle only what you expect. A catch that swallows everything hides bugs, outages and data problems. Re-throwing lets a boundary (an HTTP handler, a job runner) deal with the rest.
options: It is needed to make the function return never
Errors the block did not expect keep travelling up instead of being silently swallowed
It turns the error back into an Error object
It resets the stack trace so the log is shorter

questions.q: Why does the lesson write override readonly name = "InsufficientFundsError" instead of this.name = new.target.name?
questions.explain: Both work in plain Node.js. But bundlers and minifiers shorten class names, and then logs show e: …. A literal also gives the property a literal type, which is useful for narrowing.
options: Because new.target does not exist in TypeScript
Because a string literal makes the error faster to throw
Because minifiers rename classes, so new.target.name could become "e", while a literal survives any build
Because name cannot be assigned in a constructor

questions.q: Which class field has the literal type "card_declined" rather than string?
questions.explain: A readonly property initialized with a literal keeps the literal type, because it can never change. A mutable field widens to string, and an explicit string annotation widens it too. (A static field is not on the instance at all.)

questions.q: What is the type of error.cause for an error created with new Error("failed", { cause: dbError })?
questions.explain: ErrorOptions declares cause?: unknown, because any value may be a cause. Narrow it like a caught value, for example with instanceof Error when walking a cause chain.

questions.q: An InsufficientFundsError with a code and a shortByKobo field is sent to a worker thread, which uses structuredClone. What arrives?
questions.explain: Structured cloning keeps an error's message but only the standard error types, so a custom class arrives as a plain Error. JSON.stringify does the reverse: it keeps own enumerable fields such as code and drops message. Rely on a code string at boundaries, not on instanceof.
options: A plain Error with the message, but without the custom name, class or extra fields
A plain object with code and shortByKobo but no message

questions.q: Why does askForNewCard(new Error("db down")) compile when the parameter type is class CardExpiredError extends Error {}?
questions.explain: TypeScript is structurally typed: a class with no extra members has the same shape as its parent. Add a member with its own literal type, such as readonly code = "card_expired", and a plain Error no longer fits.
options: Because TypeScript compares shapes, and CardExpiredError declares nothing a plain Error lacks
Because instanceof checks are skipped for errors
Because function parameters are always checked bivariantly

questions.q: What turns CardDeclinedError | InsufficientFundsError | ProviderUnavailableError into a discriminated union that a switch can narrow?
questions.explain: A discriminant is a property every member has, with a different literal type in each. switch (failure.code) then narrows to the matching class, and a never default makes the check exhaustive.
options: Each has a readonly code property with its own literal type
They are declared in the same file

questions.q: In a payments service, which failure is the best fit for a returned Result rather than a thrown error?
questions.explain: A declined card is part of the business: the direct caller must decide what to show or offer, and the type should force it to. Outages, missing config and bugs are unexpected; they are thrown and handled by a boundary.
options: The database connection pool is exhausted
The customer's card was declined by their bank
A configuration file is missing at startup
A bug makes a function read a property of undefined

questions.q: You want the caller of an async function to be forced to handle a declined card. Which return type does that?
questions.explain: Promise<T> has one type parameter, for the value; a rejection cannot be typed, and TypeScript has no throws clause. Put the expected failure in the resolved value instead.

questions.q: In loadRate().catch((reason) => reason.message.toUpperCase()), what is the type of reason?
questions.explain: TypeScript's own declarations type the .catch callback parameter as any, whatever your tsconfig says. Annotate it yourself: .catch((reason: unknown) => …).
options: unknown, so the line does not compile
any, so the line compiles and can crash at runtime

questions.q: A function calls sendReceiptEmail(to); without await, and the rejection crashes the process later. What catches this mistake before it ships?
questions.explain: The compiler allows an unawaited promise as a statement. A type-aware linter reports it. A try around an unawaited call does not help: the call returns before the promise rejects.

questions.q: What does const STATUS = { … } as const satisfies Record<PaymentErrorCode, number> guarantee?
questions.explain: satisfies checks the object against the Record without widening its type, so a missing or extra code is a compile error, and as const keeps 402 instead of number. It cannot know about a class you forgot to add to the union; the runtime tests cover that.
options: That the status numbers are valid HTTP codes
That there is a status for every code (and no unknown codes), while keeping the literal numbers
That STATUS can be changed at runtime
That every error class has been added to PaymentError

questions.q: Why does the payments error system replace the message of an InternalError with a neutral sentence in the response?
questions.explain: An unexpected error's message was written for developers, not clients. The full error, with its cause chain, goes to the server log; the client gets a code and a safe sentence.
options: Because internal errors have no message
Because internal messages can leak hostnames, SQL, secrets or account data to the client
Because JSON cannot contain long messages
Because clients retry automatically when the message is neutral

questions.q: Where should a service catch and normalize errors?
questions.explain: Boundaries are where a failure must become a response, a retry or a log line. Code in between lets errors travel, or wraps them with a cause to add meaning. A catch that neither handles nor wraps is noise.
options: In every function, so nothing ever escapes
At its boundaries: the HTTP handler, the job runner, the message consumer
Nowhere: errors should always crash the process

questions.q: A test file contains // @ts-expect-error above a line. Someone changes the types and the line now compiles. What happens?
questions.explain: @ts-expect-error requires an error on the next line. When there is none, tsc reports "Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive". That turns "this must not compile" into a real, failing test.
options: The line is removed from the output
tsc reports the directive as unused, so the type test fails
The test runner skips the file

questions.q: In @zudojs/errors, BaseError.code is typed ErrorCode | string. What follows from that?
questions.explain: ErrorCode | string is effectively string: any code is allowed, because a framework cannot know the codes your application invents. The price is weaker narrowing; your own closed union gives stronger checks inside one service.
options: You can switch on code and get exhaustiveness checks
The set of codes is open, so you narrow its errors with instanceof or guards like isNotFoundError instead of an exhaustive switch
Codes are optional and usually missing
Only the codes in the ErrorCode enum may be used

questions.q: Which failure should be marked retryable and answered with a Retry-After header?
questions.explain: Only failures that may succeed later are worth retrying. A declined card or invalid input fails the same way every time, and a reused key is answered with the existing payment.
options: A request with a negative amount
The card provider is temporarily unavailable

questions.q: Old tutorials put Object.setPrototypeOf(this, new.target.prototype) in every error constructor. Do you need it in a TypeScript 7 project?
questions.explain: With native classes (ES2015 and later), subclasses of Error get the right prototype automatically. The workaround belonged to ES5 output, which TypeScript 7 refuses (target=ES5 has been removed).
options: No: it worked around instanceof breaking when compiling to ES5, and TypeScript 7 no longer targets ES5
Yes, but only for errors with a cause

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A thrown string stays a string. typeof null is "object". A RangeError is an Error, and the template prints the literal text Error(. A plain object is not an Error.

questions.explain: Without its own name, a subclass inherits "Error" from Error.prototype. LimitError sets it. The two classes are siblings, so neither is an instance of the other.
options:
Error: failed
LimitError: over limit
false

TransferError: failed
LimitError: over limit
false

Error: over limit

questions.q: An error is put on a job queue as JSON. What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.stringify includes own enumerable properties. The class fields name and code are; message and stack are own but not enumerable, so they are dropped. The message is still on the original object.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: return refund(id) hands back the promise before it rejects, so the try is already over and the catch never runs. return await refund(id) would resolve with "refund could not start".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The loop starts at the outermost error and follows cause until it reaches something that is not an Error: here undefined, after ECONNRESET.
options: charge failed <- provider call failed <- ECONNRESET
ECONNRESET <- provider call failed <- charge failed

questions.q: The checks are in this order. What does it print?
questions.explain: A DeclinedError is also an Error, so the first check catches it and the specific branch is never reached. Put the most specific class first.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Template literals accept unknown and call String(). An error becomes "TypeError: bad amount", and a plain object becomes the useless [object Object]. Narrow before formatting.
options:
failed: TypeError: bad amount
failed: [object Object]
failed: timeout

failed: bad amount
failed: sdk
failed: timeout
It does not compile: unknown cannot be used in a template literal

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: BigInt("12.5") throws a SyntaxError: the string is not an integer. The thrown string is wrapped in a new Error, whose name is "Error".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: All three checks must pass. The second error has a numeric code, and the plain object has the right code but is not an Error.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each promise has its own .catch, so the failed load resolves with -1 instead of rejecting, and Promise.all sees two fulfilled promises.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: map keeps the order of the array: the funds error first. Inside the "funds" case, failure is narrowed to FundsError, so shortBy is available.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A real error is returned untouched, so it keeps its class, name and stack. A string is wrapped in a new Error and kept as its cause.
options:
false RangeError
Error Error: timeout timeout

questions.q: Finish messageOf(value: unknown): string: an Error gives its message, a string gives itself, an object with a string message property gives that, and anything else gives "unknown error". Do not use as or any.
questions.explain: typeof value === "object" still allows null, so rule it out; "message" in value adds a message: unknown property; the last typeof narrows it to string.
questions.expected:
card expired
gateway timeout
limit reached
unknown error
unknown error

questions.q: Write InsufficientFundsError: it extends Error, has the name "InsufficientFundsError", a readonly code = "insufficient_funds", and a readonly shortByKobo: number. Its message is short by N kobo. It accepts an optional ErrorOptions second argument.
questions.explain: The literal name fixes what String(error) and logs print. Pass options on to super so a cause is kept. readonly gives code the literal type "insufficient_funds".
questions.expected:
InsufficientFundsError: short by 250000 kobo
insufficient_funds true

questions.q: The provider call throws a low-level error. Wrap it: in the inner catch, throw a new Error("card provider unavailable") with the caught value as its cause. The outer code prints the message and the cause's message.
questions.explain: The new error says what the failure means for your code; the cause keeps what actually happened. cause is unknown, so the reader narrows it with instanceof Error.

questions.q: Finish attempt: call fn; on success return { ok: true, value }, and when it throws return { ok: false, error } where error is the caught value if it is an Error, or a new Error with String(value) as the message otherwise.
questions.explain: attempt is the bridge from the throwing world to the Result world. Its error side can only be Error: after a catch you cannot know more, so any non-error value is normalized.

questions.q: Finish the STATUS table so it has an HTTP status for every failure code (declined 402, duplicate 409, provider down 503), and print the status for each error in the list.
questions.explain: satisfies Record<Failure["code"], number> makes a missing status a compile error, and STATUS[failure.code] is allowed because every code is a key. Add a fourth error class to Failure and the table stops compiling until it has a status.

questions.q: safeCapture should return "capture failed: …" when capture rejects, but the rejection escapes. Fix it so both lines print from safeCapture.
questions.explain: Without await, the function returns the promise while still inside the try, and it rejects after the try has finished. return await keeps the rejection inside the try, where the catch can see it.
questions.expected:
captured PAY-11
capture failed: payment PAY-10 expired

questions.q: Finish toAppError: return the value unchanged when it is an AppError; otherwise return a new AppError with code "internal_error", message "unexpected failure" and the original value as cause.
questions.explain: A normalizer gives every boundary one shape to work with. Known errors pass through with their data; everything else becomes an internal error that keeps the original as cause for the log.
questions.expected:
card_declined true false
internal_error false true
internal_error false true

questions.q: Finish debit so it returns a failed Result with { code: "frozen" } for a frozen wallet, { code: "insufficient_funds", shortBy } when the amount is larger than the balance, and the new balance otherwise. The loop prints one line per attempt.
questions.explain: Expected failures are part of the return type, so the caller cannot use result.value without checking ok, and shortBy is only readable after narrowing on code. Check frozen first: a frozen wallet should not report a shortfall.
